title: City money against licensed residential beds
question: Where an organization is paid to house and care for people, did the number of beds the State licenses move with the money?
finding: 10 City-paid organizations held 1,027 State-licensed residential beds at the start of 2022 and hold 968 now, while City payments to the same organizations went from $107.6 million to $147.4 million. 2 lost a tenth or more of their beds, 1 of them while City payments rose by a tenth or more; the largest loss is Catholic Charities: 77 beds to 32 (closed Leland Avenue Project (45, 2022-01)).
how: Beds are the licensed capacity of every adult residential, social rehabilitation, elderly residential, chronically-ill residential and children's residential licence the organization holds in the State licensing file of 8 November 2026. Beds at the start of 2022 are rebuilt from the same file, which lists licences closed since late 2021 with their closing dates. Money is everything the City paid the organization in fiscal years 2022 and 2026, all departments. City money is taken from the Controller's table of every payment, not from its narrower nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only. Left out of it, each picked out by the payment file's own label, are: loans; money the City collects for a benefit district and hands over (the district's own assessments); benefit-plan payments from a trust fund; and debt service. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment, which can be later than the year the payment was made.
limits: City payments cover everything the organization does, not only its licensed homes, so money and beds need not move together. Drug-treatment and detox sites are licensed by a different State department and are not in this file. A bed count is a ceiling, not occupancy, and a change in the capacity of a continuing licence would not show. A closed licence can mean a move, a merger or a change of licence type. The figure keeps grants and contracts the nonprofit-spending table lacks, emergency purchases, and aid paid through an organization (day care assistance, rent assistance paid on behalf of clients, in-home care contract payments). Part of that aid passes on to others, so it is a real City payment but not all of it is payment for the organization's own work. For the 444 organizations profiled, that leaves out $78.8 million of loans (9 organizations), $210.5 million of money the City collected for a benefit district and handed over (11 organizations) and $495.1 million of benefit-plan payments from a trust fund (1 organization), fiscal 2019 to 2026. District assessments are covered on the screen “Benefit districts: assessments in, City grants on top”, which keeps assessments and City grants apart.

rows.changes: closed Jo Ruffin Place (16, 2025-07); closed Odyssey House (10, 2025-10); opened Ferguson Place (12, 2025-07)
